item.title: Risk-Sharing Tests and Covariate Shocks: Drought, Floods, and Pests in Uganda
item.headline: Spending more after a drought can hide worsening living conditions
item.summary: Ugandan expenditure data show why risk-sharing tests must account for changing prices and shopping baskets. Conclusions depend on demand-model assumptions.

evidence.question: Do households share losses from widespread shocks?
evidence.method: Demand modeling and fixed-effects comparisons using eight survey waves, 2005–2020.

explainer.finding: Allowing different goods to respond differently to income removes the misleading appearance that adverse shocks improve welfare.
explainer.method: The author compared a total-spending test with one using expenditure composition and household demographics.
explainer.meaning: A family's food bill can rise because food costs more, even as its diet deteriorates. A bigger bill alone cannot establish better living conditions.
explainer.limits: Based on the December 2025 author manuscript. Shared-price and preference assumptions matter; an insignificant coefficient does not prove complete insurance.
